questions.question: Two customers attempt to reserve the final seat at the same time. Which design requirement should drive the initial database choice?
options: A protected write that permits at most one successful reservation
The highest advertised read throughput
A flexible document for every customer field
A cache with a long TTL
questions.explanation: The critical invariant is that one seat cannot be sold twice. A transaction or guarded conditional write should protect that decision before read throughput or schema flexibility are optimized.

questions.question: A product listing has optional attributes that usually load and change together. Price and inventory are owned by another protected service. What is the strongest starting model?
options: A document aggregate with explicit ownership of price and inventory
A cache as the only product record
A graph database because products have categories
A replica used as the product writer
questions.explanation: A document is useful when one evolving aggregate is read and changed together. It does not remove the need to name canonical owners for values such as price and inventory.

questions.question: At 12,000 requests per second with 88% catalog reads, how many requests per second are checkout or inventory writes before retries?
questions.explanation: Writes are 12% of 12,000: 0.12 x 12,000 = 1,440 requests per second. The remaining 10,560 requests are catalog reads.

questions.question: A customer refreshes an order-confirmation page immediately after checkout, but the read replica is behind. What is the appropriate response?
options: Read the confirmation from the primary or a path with a freshness guarantee
Treat the missing order as proof that checkout failed
Write the order directly to the replica
Disable replication permanently
questions.explanation: Asynchronous replicas can be stale. A read-after-write confirmation needs the authoritative writer or an explicitly guaranteed session-consistent path.

questions.question: Why is an outbox relay safer than having a request handler write both an order database and a document read model independently?
options: It ensures the read model can never lag
It records a publishable change with the authoritative transaction, so delivery can retry safely
It makes every downstream database strongly consistent
It removes the need for idempotent consumers
questions.explanation: Writing two systems independently can leave a split state if one succeeds and the other times out. An outbox commits the source change and publish record together; later delivery still requires retries and idempotent consumers.

questions.question: During primary failover, which action most directly prevents conflicting order histories?
options: Fence the old writer and promote exactly one candidate before accepting writes
Let all replicas accept writes until the old primary recovers
Use the cache as a temporary transaction coordinator
Discard any events that were not yet in the read model
questions.explanation: Failover needs a single writer. Fencing the old primary before promotion prevents split-brain writes that would create conflicting authoritative histories.
